newsitem.title: JAPAN: Main Japan opposition party pledges huge tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Main Japan opposition party pledges huge tax cuts.

text.p: Japan's main opposition party, lagging in opinion polls weeks before elections, unveiled a platform on Wednesday featuring sweeping tax cuts which its leader said would pay for themselves and propel him into power.

Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) President Ichiro Ozawa unveiled plans to dish out 18 trillion yen ($162 billion) in tax cuts by halving income and residents taxes and by trimming corporate taxes to 40 percent from the current 50 percent.

The last-ditch supply side proposals, which analysts have called budget busters that would roil bond markets, would pay for themselves by stimulating the economy and overhauling its structure, Ozawa said.

"Anyone who approaches this reform programme first by worrying about the costs will never make any changes," Ozawa told a news conference after he unveiled his party's policy platform for polls to be held on October 20.

In addition to stimulus effects from the tax cuts, Ozawa said his party would seek savings by trimming and privatising government agencies in its version of "administrative reform" -- the mantra of all parties in a mainly issue-free election.

Other mainstream parties -- including the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which built and nurtured many of the institutions reformists want to dismantle -- have echoed Shinshinto's calls for radical reform, forcing the party to tread carefully around details and budget questions, analysts said.

Shinshinto, formed in December 1994 from eight disparate parties which made up the short-lived reformist governments of 1993-94, has struggled with low approval ratings, factional infighting and tactical miscues in parliament.

Although it was the biggest winner in July 1995 elections for the upper house of parliament, recent public opinion polls show it trailing even the newly-minted Democratic Party, which has popular leaders but as yet ill-defined policies.
A survey of voters published on Tuesday by the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper gave Shinshinto a seven percent approval rating, behind the Democratic Party's nine percent and the LDP's 28 percent.

Shinshinto had 163 lower house seats in the parliament, which was dissolved last week. Some analysts say it could gain around 30 more in this month's elections -- not enough for it to form a government on its own. ($1=111.7 yen)
